name: t103_97_1
headline: Human Written
windows: And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren’t evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn’t be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one.

name: t103_97_2
headline: Human Written
windows: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: “Oh! I’m hooked again! That’s awesome I could notice it!” Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you’ll find there’s enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you’d regret later.

name: t103_97_3
headline: Human Written
windows: The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later.

name: t103_97_5
headline: Human Written
windows: Or if you do get an answer, it could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It’s often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that’s what it wants. If it tells you to do something, I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.

name: t103_97_6
headline: Human Written
windows: Remember those guards from The Urge to Escape, above? Same deal here, so get enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep. Borrowed is fine, as long as it’s from someone steady who won’t try to run your trip for you. But feeling attacked by a demon on a psychedelic is not necessarily paranoia. It can be real, and it’s also not bad unless you’re unprepared. It can be supremely empowering when you can send love and see how it fixes the situation.

name: t103_97_7
headline: Human Written
windows: Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I’d be careful with other drugs that mess with what’s real too. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it’s family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset. I can’t tell you exactly what to do about it, and nobody can tell you for sure what’s best for you. There are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can’t, get help from trusted advisors.

name: t103_97_8
headline: AI Generated
windows: Milder reactions afterward count as caution signs too, like getting confused or spaced out (dissociating) again and again. Get professional help right away if any of this is severe or risky, and especially if it keeps going or comes back while you’re sober.
Don’t suddenly quit a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, just because it might be part of the problem; have a doctor help you stop safely.

name: t103_97_10
headline: Human Written
windows: But if you’re still thinking of staking your life on the opposite claim, that death is just nothing, look into that claim first. Researchers at the University of Virginia have been collecting cases of small children who talk about a past life for about sixty years, and there’s a big pile of near-death accounts too. I don’t think any of it can tell you what dying will be like for you, but I’d read a few of those cases before betting my life on “nothing.”

name: t103_97_11
headline: Human Written
windows: My father used to tell suicidal people, “Oh, you want to kill yourself?
Now you can change what you’ve always been too afraid to change in your life, and then see if you still want to end it!” His point wasn’t that dying is wonderful.
If everything’s already on the table, what’s the change you still can’t bring yourself to make? Leaving? Quitting? Moving?

Telling your family who you really are? Those aren’t free, and you can’t always take them back, but they’re smaller than dying. Look at that life you’ve been afraid to change while you still have a human body.

name: t103_97_12
headline: AI Detected
windows: With that under you, belonging with people can get a lot less desperate.

Not all at once, but the Guide keeps watching for the moment your little one starts thinking, “If they stop liking me, I won’t belong anywhere,” and keeps reminding it that a group’s approval isn’t the deepest belonging there is. By the way, this job doesn’t have to be called the Guide.
The Wise One works, or your Inner Teacher, and “Guru” does for some people.

name: t103_97_13
headline: Human Written
windows: Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving gives way to warmth, or to feeling connected. Some feel held, in the body. Being loved can open grief, too. Someone takes care of you, and you think, “Why does this make me sad?” It can be sadness for the care that was missing. While you’re present and still choosing, stay with it. Once it’s swamping you instead of opening you, slow down (like turning the song off for the night).

name: t103_97_14
headline: Human Written
windows: Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways.

name: t103_97_15
headline: Human Written
windows: All of this happens in you, so it doesn’t matter whether they get any of it (nobody’s checking their inbox). And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can’t get back to your life, make it simpler: “I miss you, and I care.” Some of that same care can go to the part of you that’s still here.

name: t103_98_2
headline: AI Detected
windows: After the day, look at what actually happened.
If you did the Protector action(s), not feeling better right away is information to learn from. Healing is nonlinear, and sometimes standing up for yourself might make you feel worse at first.
Not doing it is harder to figure out.
Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn’t know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it.

name: t103_98_3
headline: Human Written
windows: Whichever age it picks on, saving everybody was never your job. At fifteen you probably didn’t even have your own money, or anywhere else to go. And actually, not to beat a dead horse here, but every age of you was stuck with whatever it had then, even the adult you were last year. Hindsight being 20/20 doesn’t change that.

name: t103_98_5
headline: Human Written
windows: Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, The Power of Your Other Hand. As titles go, it’s pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings. The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it’s had its say.

name: t103_98_7
headline: AI Detected
windows: Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear.
And a few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again.
A lot of people’s first guess is that they didn’t go deep enough.
I don’t think that’s it, though, and I don’t think this one failed either.
Maybe the grown-up just hasn’t come out of the exercise with you yet.
Whatever you did for your little one in there, I’d try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine.
That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations.

name: t103_98_9
headline: Human Written
windows: The Guide also points beyond itself, toward a belonging deeper than any group, one that doesn’t ask you to give up being yourself.
That might be nature, or existence itself. It might be whatever your tradition sees as ultimate.

Love can come from any of these places, and you also belong there, which is a little different. Maybe you’ve felt that outside somewhere, like you didn’t need anybody’s okay to be there. The way in is time in nature and contemplative practice, like meditation.

name: t103_98_11
headline: Human Written
windows: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo.
